meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

infoOps.desc: Information operations and strategic communications watch. Switched on for an item when a trigger event (a summit, a crisis) makes messaging and influence activity worth tracking on its own: a narrower hourly feed of reporting on official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns, plus dated findings and an assessment researched daily from open sources.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.

items.whyNow: The deep-strike war is widening on both sides while the diplomatic track stalls: on 26 Sep Russia launched 173 drones, about 50 of them jet-powered, killing two women in Zaporizhzhia and two people in Sumy, Ukraine's General Staff reported hits on the Azov optical-mechanical plant of the Tactical Missiles Corporation and the Ilsky refinery, which halted, and Zelensky said Russia will spend $12bn on jet drones and loitering munitions in 2027 against a 55% Ukrainian interception rate, while Trump declined to confirm the Patriot production licence and Zelensky said Putin 'always has some pretext' not to hold the three-way meeting.
changes: 26 Sep: Russia launched 173 Shahed-type drones overnight, about 50 of them jet-powered, with 134 downed and hits at 19 locations; two women died under the rubble of their home in Zaporizhzhia, two people were killed in Sumy and five injured in Kyiv region, while Ukrainian drones killed three in Krasnodar Krai; ArcelorMittal halted its Kryvyi Rih works after four missile strikes in five weeks killed five workers; Zelensky said 'Russia is escalating every single day' and that Putin 'always has some pretext' not to hold a three-way meeting, and Lavrov accused Europe of hindering the US-backed talks (Al Jazeera, Euronews, Kyiv Independent).

26 Sep: Ukraine's General Staff reported strikes on the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Rostov Oblast (Tactical Missiles Corporation; foundry fire, five production buildings damaged), the Ilsky refinery in Krasnodar Krai, which halted after three primary units and its tank farm were hit by FP-1 drones of the 414th Brigade, a Pantsir-S2 and a P-18 radar near Semenivske (Kyiv Independent, UNN); The Guardian reported Russian strikes on Kyiv ISPs and data centres on 23–25 Sep that cut internet to about 100,000 households and killed four at Datagroup's offices, which ISW on 25 Sep called a search for 'alternative defeat mechanisms' (Guardian via Irish Examiner, RBC-Ukraine).

26 Sep: Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence documents show Russia plans to spend $12bn in 2027 on jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, that Ukraine intercepts about 55% of jet-powered Shaheds against over 90% of conventional ones, and that 11 drone co-production agreements are signed, the latest with Finland (Kyiv Independent, single source); Trump, asked by CNN, declined to confirm the Patriot licence Zelensky announced on 25 Sep, saying only 'I want him to settle with Putin' (CNN).

25 Sep: Russian drones killed seven in Kyiv, including a 14-year-old and four at an office building in Solomianskyi, with 57 injured (Ukrinform, Kyiv Independent); Zelensky and Peskov both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks, possibly in the UAE, without a date (Al Jazeera, Ukrainska Pravda); Putin said all proposals remain on the table but Ukraine 'should be made to feel Russia's retaliatory strikes' for its election-week attacks and that Russia is 'not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe' (Meduza, Euronews); the General Staff confirmed hits on the Lukoil Perm and Novoshakhtinsk refineries, two radars and the Iskra plant in Ulyanovsk (Ukrinform, Meduza); Zelensky said Trump had made a 'final decision' on Patriot production licences (Kyiv Post) and Macron called a 300,000-man Russian mobilisation 'plausible' (Meduza).

24 Sep: Russia's night attack with 282 drones, four Zircons and three ballistic missiles killed 16 and injured 59 across Ukraine; Peskov said Moscow seeks 'peace, not a temporary ceasefire' after Lavrov on 23 Sep ruled out any pause during talks; ISW recorded no advance by either side and called Russian claims of encircling Dobropillia cognitive warfare; suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova (Kyiv Independent, ISW via Kyiv Post).

20 Sep: Operation Vivaldi phase two retook Shandryholove, Derylove and Drobysheve north of Lyman, the 3rd Army Corps crediting ground robots with 15,700 missions and 90% of frontline evacuations (single source); ISW on 25 Sep assessed that Russian claims of gains in northern Sumy are cognitive warfare intended to divert attention from Ukraine's advances north of Lyman, while recording a real Russian advance southeast of Dobropillia (Kyiv Independent, Defence Matters, ISW via Kyiv Post).

next.text: Date and venue of the US-proposed technical-level trilateral round confirmed by Kyiv and the Kremlin on 25 Sep (UAE mooted) after Zelensky's 26 Sep charge that Putin 'always has some pretext' and Lavrov's claim that Europe is obstructing; whether an energy-strike moratorium is on the agenda.
next.ifSeen: Round convened with an energy moratorium on the agenda → phase check and flag this week; no date by end-October → expect the winter energy and data-centre campaign to open unchecked.

next.text: Putin's 25 Sep 'retaliatory strikes' line translated into two or more raids of 250+ drones with ballistic waves on Kyiv in one week, or a strike package on gas production, heating plants or a third Kyiv data-centre cluster after the 23–25 Sep ISP strikes.
next.ifSeen: Escalate; the ballistic interception rate over Kyiv (60% on 24 Sep) and data-centre failover become the metrics for layered defence.

next.text: Ukraine's interception rate against jet-powered Shaheds (55% on 26 Sep per Zelensky, against over 90% for conventional drones) rises above 75% through scaled jet-drone interceptors, or jet-powered variants exceed half of a 200+ drone raid.
next.ifSeen: Rate rises → note for the monthly pattern set on interceptor drones as the primary counter; jet share exceeds half with the rate flat → escalate on the 2027 $12bn Russian programme.

next.text: The Patriot production licence Zelensky announced on 25 Sep, which Trump declined to confirm on 26 Sep, put in writing (DSCA notification or a Raytheon/Ukrainian partner announcement), and the new interceptor batch deal made public.
next.ifSeen: Confirmed → note for the monthly pattern set on sovereign interceptor production; denied or left unconfirmed by Washington → track only.

next.text: CEC final Duma results (due by 5 Oct) followed by a Russian mobilisation decree or covert call-up of the 300,000 Macron called 'plausible' on 24 Sep, or Ukraine's own mobilisation changes enacted.
next.ifSeen: Decree → escalate and phase check; no decree but regional call-up orders → monthly pattern note on force generation under attrition.

next.text: Vivaldi phase three toward the Zherebets line after Zelensky's 25 Sep 'not over' remark, or a Russian shift south toward Sloviansk; a verified Russian advance toward Dobropillia beyond the local gain ISW recorded southeast of the town on 25 Sep.
next.ifSeen: Phase check: attritional stalemate versus an operational-level shift.

next.text: Further NATO airspace incidents after the Mi-8 over Poland (23 Sep) and drone crashes in Romania and Moldova (24 Sep) despite Putin's 25 Sep denial of any plan to fight Europe; a NATO shoot-down over Poland under the raised posture, an Article 4 consultation, or the hybrid strike on a supporter state Tusk warned of.
next.ifSeen: Alliance-response dimension → escalate if a shoot-down or consultation occurs.

timeline.text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held three-hour talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, then travelled to Kyiv under a three-day pause on strikes against both capitals.
Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the pause declared during the US envoys' visit.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, followed on 22 September by strikes on the Ufa and Samara refineries more than 900 kilometres from the border.

Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly and offered a reciprocal energy ceasefire, which Lavrov answered the next day by saying Russia would not pause its operation during negotiations in any format.
Russia launched 282 drones and three waves of ballistic and Zircon missiles, killing 16 people across Ukraine including two in Kyiv, while suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova.

Russian drones killed seven people in Kyiv as Ukraine's General Staff confirmed strikes on the Lukoil Perm refinery 1,450 kilometres from the border, and Kyiv and the Kremlin both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks.

Russia launched 173 drones, about 50 of them jet-powered, killing four people, while Ukraine's General Staff reported hits on the Azov optical-mechanical plant and the Ilsky refinery and Zelensky said Russia will spend $12bn on jet drones in 2027.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status holds at the front and is contested in the information space. ISW on 25 Sep read Russian claims of encircling Dobropillia and of gains in northern Sumy as cognitive warfare meant to hide Ukraine’s elimination of the salient north of Lyman, yet also recorded a real Russian advance southeast of Dobropillia, so the 3rd Army Corps’ ravine approaches and drone saturation buy local, not operational, uncertainty. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating is borne out by the jet-drone gap: Zelensky said on 26 Sep that Ukraine downs about 55% of jet-powered Shaheds against over 90% of conventional ones, that 50 of the 173 drones launched were jet-powered, and that Russia will spend $12bn on them in 2027 (single source), while Trump declined to confirm the Patriot licence.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, both sides are widening the target set. Ukraine’s General Staff on 26 Sep reported the Azov optical-mechanical plant and the Ilsky refinery, which halted, a day after Perm and Novoshakhtinsk, while Russia hit Kyiv data centres and ISPs on 23–25 Sep, cutting internet to about 100,000 households, and missile strikes stopped ArcelorMittal at Kryvyi Rih. Geographic redundancy kept Cosmonova and Datagroup services up (single source): dispersed support working in the civil domain.

items.whyNow: Targeting and a fight over who runs aid, not implementation, set the tempo two weeks before the truce's first anniversary: on 26 Sep the IDF said strikes in Nuseirat and Khan Younis killed a Nukhba operative and another Hamas member, a further drone strike west of Nuseirat that evening killed a Palestinian as the toll since October 2023 neared 74,000, Hamas condemned the Board of Peace's 25 Sep refusal to work with UNRWA as 'complete alignment' with Israel, and Khalil al-Hayya said weapons sit inside a roadmap 'package' ending in statehood, two days after Blair told the Board that Hamas had agreed to the destruction of its tunnels and weapons factories.
changes: 26 Sep: The IDF said a strike on Nuseirat killed Ibrahim Fawzi Ismail Mohsen, a Nukhba Force member, and a Friday strike in Khan Younis killed Hamas operative Mohammed Kamel Suleiman Mohsen, both accused of restoring Hamas infrastructure 'in systematic violation of the ceasefire' (Times of Israel); Anadolu reported Mohsen, 36, was killed by a drone while visiting his brother's grave at Al-Sawarha cemetery and four were injured including a girl, with the toll 'nearly 74,000' since October 2023; on the evening of 26 Sep another drone strike on Julis Street west of Nuseirat killed a Palestinian and injured several, WAFA putting the toll at 73,914 killed and 1,394 since the truce, figures that conflict with the 73,928 and 1,408 reported on 24 Sep (Anadolu, WAFA); Al Jazeera counted seven Palestinians killed in 48 hours.

26 Sep: Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem condemned the Board of Peace's 25 Sep statement that it will 'only work with trusted partners' and that 'UNRWA's days are over' as 'complete alignment with the Zionist position' aimed at ending the agency and the right of return, and accused the Board of delivering neither aid nor ceasefire enforcement; former UNRWA chief Lazzarini said Israel keeps blocking basic aid (Al Jazeera); Khalil al-Hayya told Al-Araby that Hamas agreed last October to a roadmap that 'must be implemented as a package' from the first ceasefire phase through statehood, including 'the issue of weapons', without saying whether Hamas would disarm, and said Hamas would contest Palestinian elections in a national coalition (Times of Israel, single source).

25 Sep: An Israeli strike on a vehicle at the gate of the Wijdan displacement camp in al-Mawasi killed one Palestinian (Arab News, WAFA); the IDF said two reservists were killed on 24 Sep when their Atalef FPV drone crashed on take-off in the northern buffer zone and exploded when picked up, and it grounded all small explosive-carrying drones pending a brigadier-general inquiry that will examine Hamas electronic interference, which the IDF assesses Hamas cannot mount (Times of Israel, JNS); the IDF and Shin Bet said they have killed 16 'key' Hamas financial officers who moved over $1bn through money changers in Turkey and Gaza and will 'continue to act' (Times of Israel).

25 Sep: The New York Times corroborated Haaretz's report that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu of a 'major attack' by Hamas about a week before 7 Oct 2023, which Netanyahu's office denies (Haaretz, Times of Israel); WHO's Tedros told UNGA that Gaza still faces a public health emergency (ANHA, single source); Kallas said Gaza progress is 'far too limited' (Anadolu); a KSrelief convoy entered Gaza (SPA).

24 Sep: Netanyahu told UNGA that genocide allegations are 'the biggest lie of the century' without setting out ceasefire steps; Hamas said it is 'fully ready' to implement the roadmap and demanded entry of the technocratic committee and the international force (CBS, Jerusalem Post); at a Board of Peace event Blair said Hamas 'has agreed' to the systematic destruction of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels and weapons factories under Gaza City, Mladenov said the Board works to no timetable, and ISF commander Jeffers said 500 troops from Morocco and Kosovo have completed training with Albanian and Kazakh contingents in training, while technocratic-committee head Ali Shaath called conditions 'chaotic' and asked for winter funding (ynet, Yeshiva World, Jerusalem Post); UNCTAD put recovery needs at $71.5bn (Al Jazeera).

23 Sep: The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project six-month reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, the same day an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed Hamas finance chief Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven killed (Al Jazeera, Jerusalem Post); on 22 Sep Katz ruled out any partial withdrawal from the 63% the IDF holds until full disarmament (Jerusalem Post).

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are the biggest lie of the century, while Tony Blair told a Board of Peace event that Hamas had agreed to the destruction of its tunnels and weapons factories and Hamas demanded entry of the technocratic committee and the international force.

items.whyNow: Nothing moved on the line on 26 Sep and Cambodia's podium reply to Anutin's 24 Sep UNGA speech had still not been reported as the general debate runs to 28 Sep, so the contest sits in forums and procurement plans: Anutin pressed bilateral mechanisms and scam-and-demining cooperation from the UN, Hun Manet framed Thailand as failing to honour the December agreements in his 21 Sep peace-day message, and a 22 Sep report says the RTAF's FY2026 plan lists 20 Israeli Rampage missiles and precision kits to reach Cambodian long-range rocket launchers, while the border stays fortified, walled and closed ahead of the October Hague conciliation round.
changes: 26 Sep: No exchange of fire, incursion, drone crossing or protest note was reported on 26 Sep, and no statement by Prak Sokhonn in the UNGA81 general debate had appeared in Cambodian or Thai reporting by run time (AKP said on 21 Sep he would deliver the national statement; the debate ends 28 Sep). Cambodian analysts, among them Chey Tech, had urged Phnom Penh to use the UNGA platform to present 'evidence and documents concerning Thailand's acts of aggression' (Khmer Times, single source, published 22–24 Sep).

24–25 Sep: PM Anutin told the UNGA on 24 Sep that Thailand 'has never sought conflict' and 'is engaging in good faith', that he and Hun Manet had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally but Cambodia instead launched compulsory UNCLOS conciliation, which concerns maritime delimitation only, and urged Phnom Penh to cooperate on border security, demining and online-scam networks (Thai PBS World; Nation Thailand; Bangkok Post; Khmer Times). Cambodian analyst Nhel Rattha called the speech 'a diplomatic tactic and the creation of a political narrative' (Phnom Penh Post, single source). The Aviationist published mission markings on 19 RTAF F-16s recording Mk.82, Mk.84, GBU-12 and KGGB employment in the July and December 2025 operations (The Aviationist, 25 Sep, single source).

23–24 Sep: Hun Manet told an international anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh on 23 Sep that scam crackdowns 'should not be used as a tool to attack other countries or as a pretext for military force' (Nation Thailand; Asia News Network); Thailand's JIC chief ACM Prapas Sornchaidee replied on 24 Sep by urging implementation of Clause 10 (anti-scam cooperation) of the 27 Dec 2025 agreement, while Sihasak said the October Hague round 'will move on to the substance' and Prak Sokhonn called conciliation 'a means to rebuild trust, not a form of escalation' (Nation Thailand; Thai PBS World; Khmer Times).

22 Sep: Defence Security Asia reported that the RTAF's FY2026 procurement plan lists 20 Israeli Rampage air-launched rockets, 100 MPR-500 bombs with fuzes and 50 Lizard III laser-guidance kits for its F-16s, about US$33m, framed as a stand-off answer to Cambodia's Chinese-made PHL-03 launchers (70–130 km range); the items are planned procurements, not confirmed contracts, and Cambodia has denied preparing to use the PHL-03 (Defence Security Asia, single source). Cambodia lodged a formal protest the same day over a Buddha statue placed by Thai troops and monks on 18 Sep at Phnom Beng, Anlong Veng, calling it another 'fait accompli' on occupied land (The Star / Phnom Penh Post).

21 Sep: In his International Day of Peace message Hun Manet called peace 'the breath of life for Cambodia', urged Thailand to honour the agreements reached between the two countries and settle the border peacefully under international law, said international law alone cannot guarantee peace without political will, and contrasted stalled talks with Thailand against 86% and 84% demarcation completed with Laos and Vietnam (Phnom Penh Post; Khmer Times).

20–26 Sep: No exchange of fire, drone crossing or mine casualty was reported in the window; the last military-technical items are Cambodia's 15 Sep protest of a Thai trench near Boundary Pillar 9 and the 17 Sep Hill 450 trench settlement by liaison (Khmer Times; Khaosod English).

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.
Thai spokesman Prapas Sornchaidee warned of a full military response if Cambodian troops attacked near Chong Chom, while touring an O'Smach scam compound with ASEAN observers.
Cambodia and Thailand delivered opening statements in Singapore before a UNCLOS Annex V conciliation commission on their overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand.

The first Singapore conciliation session closed with Cambodia tabling three settlement options and Thailand insisting a maritime boundary be delimited before any resource sharing; a second meeting was set for The Hague in October.
Cambodia formally protested a Buddha statue that Thai troops and monks placed on 18 September at Phnom Beng in Anlong Veng, calling it a fait accompli on occupied land.

Hun Manet told an international anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh that scam crackdowns must not become a pretext for military force against a neighbour; Thailand replied the next day by demanding implementation of the anti-scam clause of the December agreement.

Anutin told the UN General Assembly that Thailand regretted Cambodia's turn to UNCLOS conciliation after the two leaders had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally, and urged joint work on border security, demining and scam networks.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving reading is borne out: no exchange of fire, drone crossing or mine casualty was reported between 12 and 26 Sep, the Hill 450 trench was settled by liaison on 17 Sep (single source), and the only frictions are a trench near Boundary Pillar 9 protested on 15 Sep and the Phnom Beng statue protested on 22 Sep. What is new is capability rather than behaviour: the 22 Sep report that the RTAF's FY2026 plan lists 20 Rampage rockets and precision kits to reach PHL-03 launchers (single source), and the 25 Sep reading of F-16 mission markings (single source), show Thailand institutionalising stand-off strike against long-range rockets as the lesson of 2025. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired, but consolidation under the ceasefire continues: the Chanthaburi wall's first stage stands, Thai troops hold O'Smach, and Cambodia calls each structure a fait accompli.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is confirmed while the forum has moved to New York: Anutin argued for bilateral mechanisms at the UNGA on 24 Sep, Hun Manet framed Thailand as failing to honour the December agreements on 21 Sep, and Cambodia's podium reply was still unreported on 26 Sep. No GBC or JBC has met this year; adaptability stays Low.

items.whyNow: Rodríguez left New York on 26 Sep with photographs beside Trump but no concrete deal and no election date, Trump said at the White House the same day that he had 'spoke[n] about elections' with her, Rubio said the project must 'culminate in a free and fair election', and Machado's movement answered the seventh blocked return with a nationwide caravan called for 27 Sep, so the legitimacy contest is now about the calendar. The maritime strike campaign has been silent since the 70th strike on 19 Sep, and the Pentagon-backed NABEP venture is reported to be overtaking Chevron as Venezuela's second-largest producer.
changes: 26 Sep: Rodríguez returned from the UN week with 'no concrete agreements' on debt, energy or mining and no election date, Reuters reported; Rubio said 'for this project to be successful, it culminates in a free and fair election', analysts Antonio De La Cruz ('where are the disbursements, the reconstruction package or the business deals?') and Nicmer Evans ('there will be elections, but when the United States sees fit') read the visit as modest, experts put a credible vote at least 12 months away, ExxonMobil is reported negotiating a return to Petromonagas and the IDB's $2.5bn bridge loan still faces board opposition (Reuters via Yahoo News). Trump told reporters at the White House he had spoken with Rodríguez this week: 'I did... I spoke about elections' (Reuters via Internazionale).

26 Sep: Chief government negotiator Jorge Rodríguez denied that the authorities are blocking Machado's return ('No vale, por Dios') and said parliamentary, municipal, gubernatorial and presidential elections would be held within the constitutional timeframe (El Nacional). Machado's Comando con Venezuela called a nationwide 'gran caravana' for Sunday 27 Sep at 10:00 to demand her safe return, an electoral schedule and a presidential election in 2027, saying her private flight from Panama 'never even took off' because Bonaire, Aruba and Curaçao refused landing permission (EFE via Infobae). Panama's President Mulino had said on 23 Sep her return was 'a problem for Venezuelans, not mine' (El Nacional).

26 Sep: A Wall Street Journal report, relayed by Rio Times and Voz, says the Pentagon-backed North American Blue Energy Partners produces about 220,000 b/d against Chevron's 280,000 and plans to add about 180,000 b/d next year, while Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell's statement that the Office of Strategic Capital 'does not take equity positions' contradicts the White House's 35% stake claim (Rio Times, single source on the contradiction). Rystad (24 Sep) models Venezuelan output at 1.6m b/d by 2028 and 1.8m by 2030 with NABEP's Lake Maracaibo assets near 200,000 b/d. No JTF-WHEM strike has been reported since the 70th on 19 Sep (Just Security timeline, updated 20 Sep).

25 Sep: Foreign Policy summarised Rodríguez's UN debut as a legitimacy win, with Washington working with her on oil while declining to press for elections (Foreign Policy); SDNY prosecutors opposed Cilia Flores's bail request as an 'extreme flight risk' ahead of the joint Maduro–Flores trial set for 1 Jun 2027 (De Último Minuto, single source).

24 Sep: Rodríguez and Trinidad and Tobago PM Persad-Bissessar issued a joint statement at Venezuela's UN mission on 'a new era in bilateral relations' and Venezuela declared her persona grata, reversing the 2025 declaration (Barbados Today; Nation News). Hundreds marched from Plaza Venezuela to the CNE in Caracas demanding Machado's return, new electoral authorities and a 2027 election, with no security-force response reported (EFE via Infobae); Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama on 21–22 Sep failed, seven blocked returns in all (MercoPress).

21–23 Sep: Rodríguez told the UNGA on 23 Sep 'there will be elections' in an 'orderly, institutional and verifiable' transition and thanked Trump for restoring cooperation (UN News; Al Jazeera); Chile's Kast agreed to restore ties step by step (Meganoticias; El Nacional); Rubio said the 22 Sep Trump–Rodríguez pull-aside covered restructuring about $60bn of defaulted bonds and the IDB president is drafting a two-year plan around a $2.5bn loan facing board pushback (Reuters via US News); Lula told CNN on 21 Sep the US acts as Venezuela's 'big boss' and he would call elections in her place (CNN en Español).

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.
US-backed talks between Delcy Rodríguez's interim government and an opposition delegation led by Dinorah Figuera opened in Caracas, with Jorge Rodríguez heading the government side.
The White House announced 100-year concessions on 17 Venezuelan oil fields to North American Blue Energy Partners, with the US government taking a 35 percent stake.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere struck a go-fast vessel on Caribbean narco-trafficking routes, killing four, in the 70th US counter-cartel maritime strike.

Trump held a pull-aside meeting with interim President Delcy Rodríguez at a UN General Assembly reception, their first encounter since Maduro's capture, covering debt restructuring; the same day Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama for Venezuela had failed within 24 hours, her seventh blocked return.

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Rodríguez pledged elections and a transition to 'full democracy' and said dialogue with the opposition had opened, but gave no date; Chile's Kast met her the same week to begin restoring consular ties.

Hundreds of opposition supporters marched to the National Electoral Council in Caracas demanding Machado's return, new electoral authorities and a 2027 presidential election, while Venezuela declared Trinidad and Tobago's prime minister persona grata after a 'new era' communiqué at its UN mission.

Rodríguez returned from New York with no concrete deals and no election date as Trump said he had raised elections with her, the government's negotiator denied blocking Machado, and Machado's movement called a nationwide caravan for 27 September after Bonaire, Aruba and Curaçao refused her flight landing rights.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger has not fired: US action stays at sea, the only new military move is the MQ-9 shift to SOUTHCOM reported on 18 Sep, and no strike followed the 70th of 19 Sep through 26 Sep. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status is borne out at a lower rate, two Caribbean strikes in September against the earlier weekly pace, with no reported spillover.

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is borne out and the contest has narrowed to the calendar. Rodríguez won photographs with Trump and a Trinidad 'new era' communiqué on 24 Sep but returned on 26 Sep with no deals and no date, and the same day Trump said he had spoken to her 'about elections' and Rubio said the project must culminate in a free and fair vote, so Washington is now voicing the demand it declined to press earlier in the week. Against her, Machado's seventh blocked return on 22 Sep and the 27 Sep caravan call, and for her, Jorge Rodríguez's 26 Sep promise of four elections 'within the constitutional timeframe', make the date the object of mobilisation. Reports of the Pentagon-backed NABEP closing on Chevron (single source on the equity contradiction) show the economic track outrunning the political one; adaptability stays Medium.

items.whyNow: On 26 Sep Defence Secretary Teodoro said the Ayungin rotation-and-resupply mission 'will go on' and 'will not be deterred', and that the DND had sent 'operational' recommendations to the National Security Adviser, two days after three PLAN warships and five China Coast Guard cutters turned back the MV Lapu-Lapu run about 60 nautical miles from Second Thomas Shoal; Beijing's coast guard says Manila 'broke its commitments' and that it will 'continue law enforcement' at Ren'ai Jiao, so the next run is a live trigger, while Malaysia's defence minister said on 26 Sep that Putrajaya will reinforce Sabah against a major-power clash spilling over.
changes: 26 Sep: Teodoro said 'the RORE is a Philippine mission, and we will not be deterred ... temporary setbacks, but the mission will go on', and that the DND had submitted 'operational' recommendations to the National Security Adviser; Foreign Secretary Lazaro told the UN General Assembly that disputes 'must be resolved through diplomacy and law, not violence and might' and called the 2016 award 'final and legally binding'. No US State Department or Embassy Manila statement on the 24 Sep obstruction had been found by early 27 Sep (PNA; Manila Times; Anadolu).

26 Sep: Malaysia's Defence Minister Khaled Nordin said Putrajaya will strengthen defence 'especially in Sabah' as a precaution against a clash between major powers or an 'unexpected incident' in the South China Sea spilling over, and that the Philippine-US base on Balabac, about 50 km from Banggi island, 'demanded attention' (Malay Mail; FMT; The Star).

25 Sep: the AFP and NTF-WPS said three PLAN warships, including two Type 022 missile boats, and five CCG cutters intercepted MV Lapu-Lapu and three Navy and Coast Guard escorts about 60 nm from the shoal between 8:35 pm and 11 pm on 24 Sep; a warship radioed that it would take 'compulsory measures' and the mission was discontinued at 11:08 pm without collision or injury. PCG figures differ (one PLAN warship, nine CCG and five militia ships, 15 in all) - stated as conflicting (Manila Times; Philstar; Rappler; USNI).

25 Sep: CCG spokesman Jiang Lue said the Philippines 'went back on its commitments' by sailing 'despite repeated warnings', accused Manila of staging the run during the Mid-Autumn Festival to 'sensationalise' it, and said the CCG 'will continue to conduct rights protection and law enforcement operations' at Ren'ai Jiao; China's foreign ministry held no press conference on 25 Sep and resumes on 28 Sep (China Daily; CGTN; Xinhua; PRC MFA).

24-25 Sep: China's defence ministry said the Philippine vessel made a 'lane-change cut-off' to ram CCG-21585 on 18 Sep near Xianbin Jiao and told Manila to end military ties with Taiwan; the eleven-ship, eight-nation ADMM-Plus formation (with RSN, JMSDF and USN units) worked about 45 nm from Scarborough on 23 Sep while a PLAN warship watched and ignored BRP Jose Rizal's radio invitation; the activity was scheduled to close on 26 Sep and no closing report has been found (Xinhua; Philstar; Rappler).

22 Sep: the armed forces counted 35 Chinese naval and coast guard ships at four features for 15-21 Sep (11 at Ayungin, 16 at Bajo de Masinloc, 4 at Escoda, 4 near Pag-asa), down from 48 the week before; the 22-28 Sep count, covering the obstruction, is due around 29 Sep (Palawan News; Inquirer).

findings.text: On 26 Sep 2026 Trump told reporters before leaving the White House that he and Xi 'didn't talk about it too much. Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along', adding 'he understands very much how I feel'. He neither restated the US 'does not support' formula nor accepted Xi's 'oppose independence' wording, leaving Beijing's readout as the fuller public account of the exchange.

findings.actor: US Ambassador to China David Perdue
findings.text: After the summit Perdue said 'there's no change in the Taiwan policy here. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there', citing the one-China policy, Taiwan Relations Act, three communiques and Six Assurances (reported 27 Sep). A State Department spokesperson had said on 25 Sep that policy is unchanged and the US will 'stand with' Indo-Pacific partners 'which includes Taiwan'.

On 26 Sep 2026 People's Daily's 'Zhong Sheng' commentary called Taiwan 'the core of China's core interests' and 'the first red line that cannot be crossed' in China-US relations, urged Washington to 'maintain the correct stance of opposing Taiwan independence', and cast 'constructive strategic stability' as a vision both leaders should 'transform into concrete action'. It kept Xi's summit wording in circulation after the White House fact sheet omitted Taiwan.

On 26 Sep 2026 the MAC rejected the White House fact sheet's line that the US and China 'were allies in World War II and fought side by side', saying the PRC 'did not even exist' before 1949, that the ROC was the true ally and that the CCP devoted 'one part' of its effort to fighting Japan. It also refused to let Taiwan be folded into US-China 'strategic stability' and cited PLA harassment east of Taiwan as the real threat to the status quo.

findings.actor: Taiwan MOFA (Deputy Minister François Wu Chih-chung)
findings.text: On 26 Sep 2026 Wu said 'Taiwan has no independence issue' because the ROC already has a president, a foreign minister and a premier, asking 'why would we declare independence?', and warned that framing Taiwan as 'an internal Chinese problem' would hurt its standing. To Reuters he said arming Taiwan and keeping its chip industry 'contributing to the world' are 'important US interests' and that guarantees on the pending package 'would be best'.

On 26 Sep 2026 Cheng said the summit showed Washington and Beijing 'maintaining dialogue and managing differences', that Taiwan 'need not choose' between being pro-US and pro-China, and that Lai should 'propose concrete plans to reduce cross-strait risks' and reopen dialogue. She cited Rubio's stockpile remark to argue for a 'long-term, stable and pragmatic' arms strategy, keeping the opposition's dialogue narrative in play before the November local elections.

On 26 Sep 2026 AEI's Zack Cooper said he 'cannot imagine' Trump letting the US$14 billion package through 'this month or next month' with the November China visit and December G20 looming, expecting delay into 2027 or smaller tranches; Hudson's Ken Moriyasu said arms sales remain leverage Trump may use if Beijing fails to deliver by year-end. Both read the summit as leaving Taiwan's supply hostage to the next meetings.

A Global Times English editorial on 25 Sep 2026, closing out coverage of Xi's state visit, called Taiwan 'the most important and sensitive core issue in China-US relations' and repeated Xi's hope that the US will 'uphold the correct stance of opposing Taiwan independence'. It aimed Beijing's summit line at foreign readers.

findings.actor: PLA (per ROC Ministry of National Defense)
findings.text: In the 24 hours to 06:00 on 25 Sep 2026, covering summit day, Taiwan's MND reported only 2 PLA aircraft sorties, 6 PLAN ships and 5 official ships, down from 10 sorties a day earlier. Air pressure dropped sharply while Xi was at the White House, though naval presence continued. An independent tracker also recorded 2 sorties and 11 vessels on 25 Sep.

On 25 Sep 2026 Taiwan's Foreign Ministry rejected Xi's White House remarks as Beijing's 'consistent approach of distorting facts', said the ROC and PRC 'are not subordinate to each other', and called China the 'true disruptor' of regional peace. This was a same-day rebuttal of the Chinese readout in which Xi urged the US to 'uphold the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence'.

On 25 Sep 2026 Atlantic Council's Markus Garlauskas said no public Taiwan bargain emerged, but Taiwan is not 'unaffected' because the arms package is still pending. Josh Lipsky judged the summit an optics win for Beijing because its near-equal 'G2' framing showed Washington standing 'toe to toe with China' rather than leading a coalition.

According to the PRC MFA readout of the 24 Sep 2026 White House talks, Xi told Trump that China's position on reunification is 'clear-cut' and that the US should 'adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence' and 'handle the Taiwan question with caution'. This goes beyond the long-standing US 'do not support' wording. On 25 Sep, Taiwan's MOFA rejected it as 'distorting facts and unilaterally conveying its own positions'.

assessment.text: Evidence for 24 to 27 Sep 2026 shows Beijing pressing Taiwan through the summit record rather than documented covert activity. Xi's 'oppose Taiwan independence' request (PRC MFA, 24 Sep) was carried forward by Global Times on 25 Sep and People's Daily on 26 Sep, which called Taiwan 'the first red line', while the PLA kept air activity to two sorties on summit day. Washington's messaging was ambiguous rather than aligned: the White House fact sheet omitted Taiwan, Trump said on 26 Sep only that Xi 'understands very much how I feel', and Ambassador Perdue and the State Department insisted the language is unchanged, so the wording contest is unresolved and the arms package is expected to wait for the November and December meetings. No fact-check or NSB count of inauthentic activity for this window was found. Taipei answered daily, MOFA on 25 Sep and the deputy foreign minister and MAC on 26 Sep rebutting the 'independence' and WWII framings, while the KMT's 26 Sep call for dialogue shows the domestic channel open to Beijing's narrative before the November elections.

items.whyNow: Jaishankar told the UN General Assembly on 26 Sep that 'a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this assembly' and that India's 'right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised', India's right of reply warned that 'terror will have consequences' without answering Sharif's Indus 'act of war' line directly, and Pakistan's counter-reply accused India of 'weaponising water' and exporting terrorism; the exchange stays verbal, the Line of Control is quiet, and Exercise Tarang Shakti opened at Jodhpur the same day with US F-35s.
changes: 26 Sep: Jaishankar told the 81st UNGA General Debate that 'a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this assembly', that arguments 'invoked to normalise terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences' will 'not stand' and that 'our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised'; at a press briefing he called Pakistan 'a terrorist country'. India's right of reply, delivered by First Secretary Petal Gahlot, said 'terror will have consequences', called Pakistan 'a regime of the army, by the army, and for the army', said Pakistan's military 'pleaded' for the 10 May 2025 ceasefire and reaffirmed J&K as integral, without directly answering the Indus 'act of war' line (The Tribune; ANI; Sunday Guardian; Daily Jagran).

26 Sep: Pakistan's counter-reply by Counsellor Saima Saleem accused India of having 'elevated propaganda into statecraft' and exporting terrorism 'from regional to global', cited the Kulbhushan Jadhav and Nikhil Gupta cases, called holding the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance 'weaponising water' for 240 million people and said India 'lost its credibility' in 'Marka-i-Haq' in May 2025 (Dawn).

26 Sep: Exercise Tarang Shakti opened at Jodhpur (to 12 Oct) with eight air forces deploying assets and 32 observer countries; US F-35As and a KC-135 made their first appearance in an Indian exercise, France sent seven Rafales and the UAE F-16s; the Tribune/ANI put the F-35 contingent at two to three aircraft against the six reported on 25 Sep (figures conflict) (The Tribune; ETV Bharat).

26 Sep (reported): Defence Security Asia says Pakistan has received the Turkish Baykar K2 kamikaze UAV (2,000 km-plus range, ~200 kg warhead, swarm and GNSS-denied navigation) as first export customer, with no official confirmation of numbers, delivery or readiness; The Week had reported the planned acquisition on 9 Sep (Defence Security Asia; The Week) (delivery single source).

25 Sep: Sharif told the UNGA that India's holding of the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance has 'no legal basis' and that any attempt to 'stop, impede or divert' Pakistan's share 'will be treated as an act of war', called Kashmir Pakistan's 'jugular vein', praised Munir's conduct of the May 2025 fighting and credited Trump's 'timely intervention'; Indian diplomat R. Srinivas was filmed shaking his head in the hall (Dawn; UN News; ThePrint).

23–24 Sep: India's UNHRC right of reply in Geneva said 'neither terror nor theatrics' would repay Pakistan's loans; New Delhi restated that the Indus Court of Arbitration is constituted in contravention of the treaty; Dar told the OIC Contact Group India 'cannot set aside international obligations when inconvenient'; three landmines were defused near the LoC in Poonch and no cross-border firing has been reported in the window (The Week; News On AIR; Dawn).

timeline.text: A Hague Court of Arbitration unanimously rules the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and bars India from raising the Ratle dam; India rejects the award within hours as 'illegally constituted'.
Pakistani troops fire small arms and mortars across the Line of Control in Poonch's Mankote sector, a day after firing in Krishna Ghati; the Indian Army retaliates.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025, and each side summons the other's charge d'affaires the next day.
Two Pakistani Jaish-e-Mohammad militants are killed overnight in 'Operation Sohan' in the Majalta forests of Udhampur, Jammu, and a suspected over-ground worker is detained.
India rejects Pakistan's version of the warship collision as 'the usual prevarication', insisting INS Kolkata was on routine surveillance in international waters.

India's envoy at the UN Human Rights Council tells Pakistan that 'neither terror nor theatrics' will repay its loans, New Delhi restates that the Indus arbitration court is illegally constituted, and Dar tells the OIC Contact Group that the treaty is binding under the August award.

Sharif tells the UN General Assembly that any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan's share of the Indus waters 'will be treated as an act of war', calls Kashmir Pakistan's 'jugular vein' and credits Trump's intervention in the May 2025 conflict, while an Indian diplomat shakes his head in the hall.

Jaishankar tells the General Assembly that 'a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts' and that India's right to defend itself 'will be exercised', India's right of reply warns that 'terror will have consequences', and Pakistan's counter-reply accuses India of 'weaponising water' and exporting terrorism, as Exercise Tarang Shakti opens at Jodhpur with US F-35s.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status held without a kinetic test: the 15 Sep Arabian Sea collision has not recurred, no Line of Control firing has been reported since the 11 Sep Mankote incident (single source) and the only border activity was three mines defused in Poonch on 23 Sep. Signalling has moved to exercises and munitions: Tarang Shakti opened at Jodhpur on 26 Sep with US F-35As near the Pakistan border, and a 26 Sep Defence Security Asia report of Pakistan receiving the 2,000 km Baykar K2 kamikaze drone (single source) would, if confirmed, add a conventional deep-strike option below the nuclear threshold. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established rating was reinforced verbally on 26 Sep when Jaishankar told the General Assembly that India's 'right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised' and Gahlot's right of reply warned that 'terror will have consequences' ahead of the autumn infiltration season.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested edge is now a two-sided information contest: Sharif's 25 Sep Indus 'act of war' line was answered on 26 Sep not on water but on terrorism, while Saleem's counter-reply framed abeyance as 'weaponising water' and May 2025 as a Pakistani victory. Neither side moved a red line, so adaptability stays High but unexercised.

changes: 26 Sep: On the Rakhine–Ayeyarwady border the AA-led coalition is pressing Theaphyu, Thabaunglay and Kinmunchin (Thabaung) and is within a mile of the junta's Artillery Battalion 344 in Yegyi; residents say convoys carrying 'hundreds' of killed and wounded reach Pathein's Medical Corps 4 nightly, with a tactical operations commander and a major among the dead, while LID 66 under Southwestern Command mounts a counter-offensive across Laymyethna, Yekyi and Thabaung with air and artillery support and executed a 21-year-old civilian near Pandawgyi on 21 Sep (BNI/DMG) (single source, casualty scale unverified).

26 Sep: An MNDAA delegation led by the group's general secretary has been in Naypyidaw since 23 Sep for talks with the junta's National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee from 24 Sep on reopening China–Myanmar border trade routes; the trip nearly collapsed after junta reconnaissance flights over MNDAA-held Kutkai and Theinni and went ahead only after Beijing pressed the Brotherhood Alliance (BNI) (single source).

26 Sep: Conscription pressure is visibly expanding: Mon State's 28th intake press-ganged 222 men, many seized for curfew breaches or from public spaces, with militias extorting exemption fees and selling those who cannot pay to administrators for bounties; RFA's 20 Sep investigation counts 28 batches and 130,000-plus recruits since February 2024, with a trafficking market of 10–30 million kyat per recruit; CNA headlined the drive's expansion (headline only) (BNI/IMNA; RFA; CNA).

26 Sep: DVB confirmed the regime recalled its ambassador to Thailand, Zaw Zaw Soe, to Naypyidaw for interrogation over trafficking of migrant workers via Kawthaung and embassy passports and visas issued to exiled opponents, resolving last run's single-source flag; a 24 Sep airstrike and shelling on Bawlakhe, Karenni, killed two civilians and wounded four including a four-year-old, taking September's Karenni civilian air-strike toll to at least 12 (DVB; BNI/Kantarawaddy Times).

25 Sep: Justice For Myanmar welcomed EU Advocate General Tamara Ćapeta's opinion, on an Austrian court's reference over trainer aircraft, a simulator and production technology exported via a civilian trader to the Myanmar Air Force (three aircraft delivered before the 2020 application), that civilian-design aircraft can fall under military export controls; Reuters confirmed that a Delhi court on 24 Sep let Matthew VanDyke and six Ukrainians leave India for a month after the NIA downgraded the drone-training case to immigration offences (Justice For Myanmar; Courthouse News; Reuters/Yahoo).

24–25 Sep: Junta attacks near Bago's 115-Mile rest stop killed seven and displaced 1,000-plus, a day after three jets bombed the NUG's Special Military Region headquarters at Kyaikto (4–10 dead, figures conflict); in Rakhine the Arakan Army says it repulsed renewed 'Operation 4926' wave attacks at Sittwe, Natyaykan and Mindon on 22 Sep with drone and sniper fire, recovering 50-plus junta bodies, and took two more Sittwe outposts on 23–24 Sep (People's Spring via Burma Coup Resistance Notes; single source); the 1,000-troop DDI 25 column has still not moved on Mindat or Kanpetlet (Myanmar Now; IMNA; BNI).

A junta column of over 180 vehicles and about 1,000 troops with MLRS, drones and signal jammers reaches the DDI 25 weapons plant in Saw Township to renew the offensive on Mindat and Kanpetlet in southern Chin State.

The Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt to breach the Maei mountain pass at Mindon into Rakhine, Malaysia sets a 29 Sep date to begin deporting Myanmar migrants after Anwar invites Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit, and Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand for questioning.

Three junta jets bomb the National Unity Government's Special Military Region headquarters in Kyaikto near the Mon–Bago border, killing between four and ten resistance personnel, as a Delhi court lets the American and six Ukrainians accused of drone training for Myanmar insurgents leave India and an MNDAA delegation opens talks in Naypyidaw on reopening China–Myanmar border trade under Chinese pressure.

Residents on the Rakhine–Ayeyarwady border report the junta trucking hundreds of killed and wounded nightly from the Thabaung front to Pathein as the Arakan Army-led coalition closes on Artillery Battalion 344 at Yegyi.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds and failed ground pushes answered from the air are visible on four fronts: the Mindon-to-Ann attempt cost LID 55 two battalion commanders on 20–23 Sep (single source), the 22 Sep wave attacks at Sittwe, Natyaykan and Mindon were broken by drone and sniper fire (single source), the DDI 25 column has not moved on Mindat, and residents on 26 Sep described nightly casualty convoys from Thabaung to Pathein (single source). The regime's answers were the 24 Sep Kyaikto and Bawlakhe strikes and, on 26 Sep, evidence that conscription is the substitute for lost infantry: Mon State's 28th intake press-ganged 222 men and RFA counts 130,000-plus recruits. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is borne out by junta drone overwatch denying rescue at Kyaikto and by the 25 Sep Reuters confirmation that India has let the foreign drone trainers go with only immigration charges.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced by external actors shaping corridors: Beijing forced the MNDAA to Naypyidaw on 23–24 Sep to talk border trade (single source), Bangladesh seized Rakhine-bound urea on 24–25 Sep, and Malaysia's 29 Sep deportation flight looms. Adaptability stays High; the transferable lesson is that airpower and coerced manpower cannot convert into held ground.

items.whyNow: Early on 26 Sep the Saudi-led coalition intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait, home of King Khalid Air Base, and two drones headed for Riyadh, the second salvo in three days after the six ballistic interceptions over Taif and Yanbu on 24 Sep; Houthi media reported Saudi strikes on Taiz the same day, the GCC called the attacks a grave escalation, and Saudi foreign minister Faisal bin Farhan told the UN General Assembly the kingdom rejects the use of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab as instruments of pressure and welcomed a 25 Sep Security Council condemnation of the Houthi attacks. Singapore-bound routings still depend on a Houthi-controlled Bab al-Mandab and a Yanbu terminal awaiting French air defence, with coalition forces in Iraq down to Erbil airport before the 30 Sep exit.
changes: 26 Sep: From about 04:00 local time coalition spokesman al-Maliki announced the interception of two Houthi drones headed for Riyadh and two ballistic missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait, the King Khalid Air Base city from which Saudi F-15s fly over Yemen; civil defence issued alerts for Khamis Mushait and Abha but none for Riyadh and no damage was reported; Houthi-run Al-Masirah reported Saudi strikes on Taiz later on Saturday (single source) (Arab News, The National, Reuters via Haaretz, CNBC).

26 Sep: GCC secretary general Al Budaiwi called the attempted attacks on Riyadh and Khamis Mushait a 'grave escalation' and 'a serious breach of the kingdom's sovereignty' and called for unified Gulf support of Saudi defensive measures; Saudi foreign minister Faisal bin Farhan told the UNGA that the kingdom rejects the use of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab 'as an instrument of pressure, threat or harm', condemned 'flagrant' Iranian and Houthi attacks and welcomed a Security Council condemnation on 25 Sep of Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia (Asharq Al-Awsat, Anadolu, The National, Arab News, Al Arabiya).

26 Sep: Iranian President Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that Houthi actions are 'not connected to Iran' and offered to mediate between the Houthis and Riyadh, while Iran's seven-day plan asks for a ceasefire covering Yemen; Al Jazeera's explainer on al-Alimi's mobilisation put Houthi strength at roughly 350,000 fighters on UN expert estimates, said the Houthis had written to the EU promising not to target EU-linked ships to isolate Saudi Arabia, and reported no significant defections under the amnesty that opened on 26 Sep (Al Jazeera).

26 Sep: Iraq said it reached an understanding with Washington to continue dollar cash shipments, with a new delivery expected soon, days before the 30 Sep coalition exit; no new attack on Erbil and no Israel–Syria development was reported on 26 Sep (Times of Israel live).

25 Sep: Yemen's President al-Alimi called for general mobilisation and offered Houthi defectors amnesty from 26 Sep; the Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani chiefs of staff met in Riyadh under the Makkah pact and agreed to deepen military and intelligence cooperation and integrate defensive capabilities; UNICEF counted about 130,000 displaced in three weeks; government forces took Jabal Nouman in Lahj after holding Kahboub for almost a week; PM Sharif told the UNGA that any threat to Makkah or Madinah is a 'red line' (France 24, Arab News, Al Jazeera, Dawn).

24 Sep: The Houthis fired ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh, the coalition intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu as sirens sounded around Makkah, Macron said France will send soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect the Yanbu terminal without giving numbers or dates, 80 UN member states condemned the Houthi resumption of the war and Red Sea attacks, and The National counted 27 Bab al-Mandab crossings; the Houthis claimed 408 crossings between 11 and 21 Sep (Anadolu, Defense News, Reuters via US News, The National, Xinhua).

next.text: Arrival and first engagement of the French radar and air-defence detachment at Yanbu (Macron gave no numbers or dates on 24 Sep); whether Rafales, UK, Italian, Greek or Gulf assets join and whether the Houthis attack the deployment itself.

next.ifSeen: Batteries or a joint command deployed → note for the monthly pattern set on coalition point defence; nothing beyond communiqués → pact remains political.

next.text: A Houthi launch that leaks through Saudi defences and hits Khamis Mushait or Taif air bases, Yanbu or Riyadh, or a launch rate above one salvo a day sustained for a week, against the current pattern of full interception at intervals of two days.
next.ifSeen: Leak-through with damage or casualties → escalate the same day; sustained daily salvos → note interceptor consumption for the monthly pattern set.

next.text: Effect of al-Alimi's general mobilisation and the amnesty opened 26 Sep: reported enlistment drives, tribal levies joining the Al-Sabiha and Taiz fronts, or notable Houthi defections (Al Jazeera reported none by 26 Sep).
next.ifSeen: Verified defections or new brigades at the front → note for the monthly pattern set; no visible effect → treat as declaratory.

ignore.note: The 26 Sep interceptions are multi-sourced through the coalition spokesman; the live-feed headlines about 'six ballistic missiles' and Makkah sirens refer to the 24 Sep salvo over Taif and Yanbu, not to 26 Sep. The Saudi strikes on Taiz on 26 Sep rest on Houthi-run Al-Masirah via Reuters. The 25 Sep Security Council condemnation is reported through the Saudi foreign minister's speech. The Houthi letter to the EU and the 350,000-fighter estimate come from Al Jazeera's explainer only. timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.
Drones launched from Iraq's Maysan province hit Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline in Riyadh and Medina provinces; Riyadh shuts the line the next day and Brent tops $100.
Houthi forces seize Perim Island and the last stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast a day after taking Mocha, gaining control of Bab al-Mandab and reiterating a ban on Saudi ships.
The Houthis fire a ballistic missile and drones at Riyadh for the first time in this escalation; Saudi Arabia says it was intercepted as smoke rises near King Khalid airport.

Ahead of the 30 September coalition exit from Iraq, the prime minister moves militia disarmament to a phased plan ending in June 2027 behind a 90-day halt in attacks, as Syrian President Sharaa says security talks with Israel reached about 90 percent before Israel pulled back.

After the Houthis fire a mixed missile and drone barrage at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh and Saudi Arabia intercepts six ballistic missiles, President Macron announces French soldiers, radars and air-defence systems for the Yanbu terminal and the Makkah pact foreign ministers agree in New York to convene their chiefs of staff.

Yemen's President al-Alimi declares general mobilisation and an amnesty for Houthi defectors as the Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani chiefs of staff meet in Riyadh and agree to integrate defensive capabilities under the Makkah pact.

The coalition intercepts two Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at the Khamis Mushait air base and two drones headed for Riyadh, the GCC calls the attacks a grave escalation, and Saudi Arabia tells the UN it welcomes the Security Council's condemnation of the Houthi strikes.

text: On long-range attack versus layered protection, the Rising · Contested status is borne out. Houthi launches at Saudi cities came on 19, 24 and 26 Sep; the 26 Sep salvo paired two ballistic missiles at Khamis Mushait, the King Khalid Air Base city, with two drones at Riyadh, a base-plus-capital pattern that tests interceptor stocks; the coalition again reported full interception and no damage. The answer remains institutional: France’s Yanbu detachment announced on 24 Sep still had no numbers or dates, the Makkah-pact chiefs of staff on 25 Sep integrated capabilities without naming a battery, and on 26 Sep the GCC and the Saudi foreign minister sought condemnation at the UN rather than new force. On maritime disruption versus route resilience, the Established · Contested status holds with a new discriminating element: the Houthis told the EU they would spare EU-linked ships (single source) and claimed 408 Bab al-Mandab crossings over 11–21 Sep, while Pezeshkian on 26 Sep disowned Houthi decisions and offered mediation, making the blockade a Saudi-specific instrument that leaves Singapore-bound routings open but exposed to that distinction.

On regional basing versus militia targeting, the Established · Contested status is shifting toward host-nation management: coalition forces sit only at Erbil airport ahead of the 30 Sep exit, Baghdad’s 26 Sep dollar-shipment understanding shows US leverage moving to financial levers, and Israel–Syria stays at Sharaa’s 90 percent (single source).
